sentences.text: Wingegyps was a small bird, even smaller than the black vulture, making its extremely tiny size the most prominent feature distinguishing it from other vultures and condors.
In Wingegyps, the foramen magnum opens entirely posteriorly and the occipital condyle is fully visible from the side, a trait that differs from other condors where this bone is often obscured.
The species name cartellei honors Brazilian paleontologist Castor Cartelle for excavating the site of the holotype — the specimen the species is based on.
The generic name Wingegyps combines the Greek word for vulture with 'Winge' to honor Danish ornithologist Oluf Winge.
The first remains assigned to Wingegyps were discovered by Danish scientist Peter Wilhelm Lund in Brazil.
Fossils of Wingegyps have been found in the states of Minas Gerais and Bahia in Brazil, as well as in Venezuela.
If Wingegyps lacked the sense of smell like its close relatives in the genus Cathartes, it would have struggled to compete with them for small carcasses.

Wingegyps may have been ecologically equivalent to the palm-nut vulture, feeding on the soft mesocarp of the Paraguay nut, or alternatively, it may have subsisted on scraps left by larger vulture species, similar to the Egyptian vulture.

Alvarenga and Olson propose that Wingegyps may have behaved similarly to specialized Old World vultures like the Egyptian vulture or palm-nut vulture, favoring the scavenging hypothesis over frugivory because Wingegyps went extinct with South American megafauna while palm trees remain widespread.
The genus Wingegyps and the species Wingegyps cartellei were both described by Alvarenga and Olson in 2004.
The morphology of the Wingegyps cranium suggests affinities with the major branch of vultures that includes the Andean and Californian condors.
Degrange and colleagues consider king vultures to be an intermediate form between vultures and condors, but not true condors.
The North American Classification Committee of the AOU and the International Ornithological Congress adopted the classification of Wingegyps within the order Accipitriformes.
Wingegyps lived during the Late Pleistocene, specifically within the Ensenadan and Lujanian stages.
Wingegyps likely lived during the Late Pleistocene or Early Holocene, with a time range estimated from 0.129 to 0.0117 million years ago.
It is debated whether Wingegyps fed on fruit or scavenged scraps to avoid competition with larger vultures, as its precise ecology remains unclear.

The taxonomic position of the family containing Wingegyps is debated, with authors placing it in Falconiformes, Ciconiiformes, Cathartiformes, or Accipitriformes. It is also debated whether Wingegyps went extinct because it relied on large carcasses that disappeared alongside American megafauna.
